papers.title: Immersive virtual reality in learning physics: a systematic review of opportunities and challenges
papers.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) can heighten presence and enable active, embodied interaction in realistic 3D environments, which has been associated with potential benefits in physics education. This article presents a comprehensive review of IVR implementation in physics education at both school and university levels. The analysis included 34 studies indexed in Scopus and ERIC, published between 1 January 2018 and 1 June 2025. Methodologically, this review followed a preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses approach. IVR implementations for physics learning were assessed, topic-aligned activity types were summarized, and associated opportunities and challenges were documented. Findings indicate that IVR can support physics learning by providing complementary visualizations, optimizing cognitive load, enabling haptic learning, saving time, and fostering collaborative inquiry. Conversely, the most frequent potential IVR challenges include discomfort, unreliable interaction, orchestration issues, relatively high costs, and significant extraneous cognitive load.

papers.title: Working with writing experts to enhance a physics curriculum
papers.abstract: A common observation of physics faculty and professionals hiring physics graduates is that undergraduate students have deficient physics-specific writing skills, in particular difficulties with writing genres such as abstracts, reports, articles, proposals, and posters. Students are not often exposed to such authentic writing experiences as part of their curriculum, and faculty may not feel qualified to teach writing. Scholarship focused on writing transfer, defined as the ability to apply the writing skills and knowledge learned in one context in a new writing context, suggests that students need support with transfer-focused writing skills such as genre and audience awareness and that these are skills in which students can be trained. For physics students, physics faculty are best placed to do this as successful participants in their disciplines. We present an interdisciplinary effort, by faculty of physics and writing studies, of developing a writing in physics curriculum using a scaffolded approach including three courses in the second through fourth year of an undergraduate physics program. This approach uses threshold concepts from writing studies, such as genre, audience, and purpose. Students are given the methodological tools to approach writing, and the instruction includes structured peer feedback that is connected to the instructor's feedback and grading. This effort led to improvements in the written and oral communication skills of students in a broad range of genres and for various audiences, evidenced, for instance, by an increase in successful fellowship applications. The course materials developed for this effort are publicly available to the community.

papers.title: Microstate Response Model: A Unified IRT Framework from Latent Nominal States to a Theory of Tests
papers.abstract: Several features outside of the conventional assumptions in traditional item response theory (IRT) models have been revealed to be related, yet no unifying framework explains the features simultaneously. They can be unified by treating each cause as a distinct reason, and then regarding every reason as a choice in a latent multiple-choice item. Here, we propose the Microstate Response Model (MiRM), which decomposes each response category (macrostate) into multiple latent reasons (microstates) using Boltzmann weights. The consequences of this simple framework are substantial; for example, it reads the lower and upper asymptotes of item characteristic curves (ICCs) as additional states, and ICC asymmetry and item complexity as multiple states. The model unifies many classical models from the dichotomous logistic family to mixture models. Moreover, the algebra of the model provides the intuition that items and tests are the same object. Two consequences naturally come out: partial credits and test scores are unified, and a new test-level monotonicity condition is proposed. We examine item characteristics including nonmonotonicity on PISA 2015, and show that MiRM provides a deeper understanding of items while achieving the strongest overall performance across fit, parsimony, and prediction.
